title: Reading the labour market: unemployment, participation and the Phillips curve
dek: The unemployment rate is the most watched number in economics, but on its own it tells you surprisingly little. Here is how to read the rest of the picture.
html:
On the first Friday of most months, traders around the world stop what they are doing at 8.30 in the morning New York time. The US jobs report is out, and within seconds bond yields, the dollar and share prices can all lurch in response to a single number: how many jobs the American economy added last month. In the UK, the equivalent release from the Office for National Statistics arrives mid-month with less fanfare but similar importance for the Bank of England. Why does the labour market matter so much? Because jobs are where most people meet the economy. They determine household incomes, they drive spending, and they hold the key to whether inflation will settle or flare up. But reading the labour market well means looking past the headline unemployment rate to a whole dashboard of other measures.

Who counts as unemployed?

You might think "unemployed" just means "without a job". It doesn't. Most countries follow the definition set by the International Labour Organization (ILO). To be counted as unemployed, you must:

  1. Be without work,
  2. Have actively looked for work in the past four weeks, and
  3. Be available to start within the next two weeks.

Someone who has a job, even for just one hour a week, counts as employed. Someone with no job who is not looking, perhaps because they are studying, caring for family, long-term sick or retired, is economically inactive. They are outside the labour force entirely.

The labour force is everyone who is either employed or unemployed. The unemployment rate is the unemployed as a share of the labour force, not of the whole population. That distinction matters. If a jobless person gives up looking, they move from unemployed to inactive, and the unemployment rate falls, even though nothing good has happened.

These figures mostly come from large household surveys rather than from benefit records. In the UK, that is the Labour Force Survey; in the US, the Current Population Survey; in the euro area, national surveys harmonised by Eurostat. Surveys have their own problems. Since 2023 the UK Labour Force Survey has suffered from sharply falling response rates, leaving the ONS to warn that its figures are less reliable than usual while it develops a replacement. It is a useful reminder that even the most-watched statistics are estimates, with margins of error.

The other numbers worth watching

Employment and participation

The employment rate is the share of working-age people (usually 16 to 64) who have a job. The participation rate (or activity rate) is the share who are in the labour force at all. These capture what the unemployment rate misses: people who have drifted out of work altogether.

The US offers a striking example. Its participation rate fell from about 67% around 2000 to below 63% in the mid-2010s. Part of that was ageing, as baby boomers retired, but part was prime-age adults, especially men without degrees, dropping out of the labour force. The unemployment rate alone gave no hint of this.

Inactivity and the UK's sickness problem

In the UK after the pandemic, the striking story was a rise in inactivity among working-age adults, driven especially by long-term sickness. The number of people inactive because of long-term ill health rose to roughly 2.8 million by 2023-24, a record on the ONS's figures, with mental health conditions and musculoskeletal problems prominent. This has become a major policy concern, both because it limits the economy's capacity to grow and because of what it costs in benefits.

Vacancies

The number of job vacancies, or openings, tells you about demand for workers. A useful summary is the ratio of vacancies to unemployed people, a rough measure of how "tight" the market is. When there are many more jobs than jobseekers, employers have to compete harder for staff, typically by raising pay.

Economists often plot vacancies against unemployment to draw a Beveridge curve, named after William Beveridge, the architect of Britain's welfare state. Normally, when vacancies are high, unemployment is low and vice versa. If the curve shifts outwards, with more vacancies and more unemployment at the same time, it can be a sign that workers and jobs are poorly matched: the wrong skills, in the wrong places.

Wages

Pay growth is the hinge between the labour market and inflation. Analysts watch average earnings, but they are noisy: if lots of low-paid workers lose their jobs, average pay rises simply because of who is left. Measures such as the US Employment Cost Index, or the Atlanta Fed's tracker of pay growth for the same individuals over time, try to strip out those composition effects. What matters ultimately is real wages, pay after adjusting for inflation, which determine living standards.

The US payroll count

The famous US jobs number, nonfarm payrolls, comes from a different source: a survey of employers rather than households. It counts jobs rather than people, is larger and more precise month to month, but is heavily revised. Economists watch both surveys and are wary when they tell different stories.

The Phillips curve: from discovery to doubt

In 1958, the New Zealand economist William Phillips, working at the London School of Economics, published a study of British data from 1861 to 1957. He found a strikingly stable relationship: when unemployment was low, money wages tended to rise quickly; when unemployment was high, wages rose slowly or fell. Others soon recast this as a link between unemployment and price inflation.

The Phillips curve seemed to offer policymakers a menu. Want lower unemployment? Accept a bit more inflation. Want lower inflation? Tolerate more joblessness.

The original Phillips curve suggested a permanent trade-off between jobs and inflation. The experience of the 1970s showed that, at least in the long run, there isn't one.

The natural rate and NAIRU

In 1967 and 1968, Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps independently argued that the menu was an illusion. If a government tried to hold unemployment permanently low by stimulating demand, workers would come to expect higher inflation and bargain for higher wages to compensate. Inflation would keep ratcheting upwards. In the long run, unemployment would return to its natural rate, determined by things like how efficiently jobs and workers are matched, the benefit system and the bargaining power of firms and unions, not by how much inflation the government tolerated.

The 1970s seemed to vindicate them. Many economies suffered stagflation: high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, which the simple Phillips curve said should not happen.

A related idea is the NAIRU, the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment: the level of unemployment consistent with stable inflation. Push unemployment below it, and inflation tends to rise; let it drift above, and inflation tends to fall. Central banks still use estimates of the NAIRU, but they are uncertain and move over time. In the UK, estimates fell from around 7% or more in the 1990s to roughly 4% to 4.5% before the pandemic, according to the Bank of England and others. Economists debate whether the NAIRU has risen since.

The flattening

In the 2010s, a new puzzle appeared. Unemployment fell to very low levels in the US, the UK and Germany, yet inflation stayed stubbornly low, often below the 2% targets. The Phillips curve, it seemed, had become very flat: big changes in unemployment barely moved inflation.

Explanations included:

  • Anchored expectations. Because people trusted central banks to keep inflation around 2%, wage and price setters no longer reacted much to short-term pressures.
  • Globalisation and competition from imports, which restrained prices.
  • Weaker worker bargaining power, with lower union membership and more insecure work.
  • Measurement problems, such as underestimating spare capacity among people who wanted more hours.

Some economists went further and suggested the relationship had all but died. Then the pandemic happened.

Worked example: the great post-pandemic tightness

After the lockdowns of 2020, economies reopened rapidly, boosted by large government support and low interest rates. Demand for workers surged, especially in hospitality, retail and logistics. Supply did not keep up. Some older workers retired early, some people were ill, and in the UK the end of free movement after Brexit reduced the flow of EU workers.

The result was the tightest labour markets in decades.

IndicatorUnited StatesUnited Kingdom
Unemployment rate, low pointabout 3.4% (2023)about 3.6% (2022)
Vacancies, peakabout 12 million (2022)about 1.3 million (2022)
Vacancies per unemployed person, peakabout 2about 1

In the US, there were roughly two job openings for every unemployed person in early 2022, a record. The euro area, too, saw unemployment fall to record lows of around 6.5% by 2023-24, despite much weaker growth.

Inflation surged at the same time, peaking at about 9% in the US in mid-2022, around 11% in the UK in October 2022 and over 10% in the euro area that autumn. Much of that came from energy and food prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine and from tangled supply chains. But tight labour markets mattered too, especially for services inflation, which tracks wages closely.

Research since then, including work by Ben Bernanke and Olivier Blanchard in 2023, suggests that the Phillips curve was not dead but non-linear: flat when the labour market has plenty of slack, but steepening sharply once vacancies run far ahead of jobseekers. The 2010s simply never got tight enough to see it.

There was a further twist. In the US, the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio fell back significantly during 2023 and 2024 without the big rise in unemployment many had feared. Some economists read this as evidence that cooling vacancies, rather than job losses, could bring wage growth down: a "soft landing" route that the traditional Phillips curve did not anticipate. In the UK, unemployment did drift up in 2024 and 2025, to somewhere near 5%, though the survey problems make the exact level unusually uncertain.

Common pitfalls when reading the numbers

  • Treating one month as a trend. Monthly changes are noisy, and revisions can be large. Look at three-month averages.
  • Ignoring inactivity. A falling unemployment rate can mean people giving up, not finding work.
  • Confusing job counts with people. One person with two part-time jobs counts twice in payrolls.
  • Forgetting population growth. An economy with fast-growing population, perhaps through immigration, needs to add many more jobs each month just to keep unemployment steady.
  • Over-trusting the NAIRU. It cannot be observed directly, and estimates can be wrong by a percentage point or more.
  • Reading nominal wages as living standards. A 6% pay rise in a year of 10% inflation is a cut in real terms.

Key takeaways

  • To be unemployed you must be out of work, looking and available. People who have stopped looking are "inactive", so the unemployment rate can fall for bad reasons.
  • Participation, inactivity, vacancies and real wages fill in what the headline rate leaves out. In post-pandemic Britain, rising long-term sickness was a central story.
  • The Phillips curve links low unemployment with higher inflation, but Friedman and Phelps showed there is no permanent trade-off; the natural rate or NAIRU is the level consistent with stable inflation.
  • The curve looked flat in the 2010s, but the 2021-23 episode suggests it steepens sharply when labour markets become very tight.
  • Survey problems, revisions and noise mean labour market data should be read as a whole and over several months, never from a single figure.
